newsitem.title: INDIA: India shares weaker as search for coalition starts.
newsitem.headline: India shares weaker as search for coalition starts.

text.p: Indian shares fell on Saturday morning as bickering politicians tried to stitch together a new coalition and avert snap polls after the United Front government was defeated in a confidence vote overnight, brokers said.
Nerves soon settled after a jittery open of the special trading sessions arranged to give investors a chance to react to Friday night's confidence vote.
Declines never developed into panic selling as players eyed the fluid political situation, having already discounted the government's defeat.

Congress party chief Sitaram Kesri told Reuters in New Delhi his party's top priority was to avoid elections after prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government lost a trust vote in parliament.
But Deve Gowda's United Front said it will not support efforts by either Congress, or the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to form a government.

Analysts saw a glimmer of hope for the markets if elections were avoided. Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive at Daewoo Securities said he foresaw a good chance of Congress and UF patching together a government, in which the parties on the left of the outgoing coalition would drop out.
The left parties were primarily opposed to liberalisation and without them the process of reform will move at a much faster pace, he said.
"It is a hope-driven market," said Ramakrishna Iyer, equity salesman at brokerage ASK-Raymond James Securities India Ltd. "The market will stay in trading range of 100 points."
At 0710 GMT, the 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index was down 53.34 points, or 1.47 percent, at 3,580.39.
The National exchange index was 13.70 points, or 1.35 percent, lower at 999.70.
The Calcutta share index was up 2.73 points, up 2.71 percent, at 103.30.
A consensus agreement among politicians to see through a widely acclaimed budget also held out hope for the markets, analysts said.

The speaker of the Lok Sabha (lower house of parliament) has fixed a three-day debate between April 21 and 23 to approve the tax and tariff cutting budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March), held hostage by the political crisis.
"There's an across-the-board support for the budget," Iyer said. "It will rejuvenate the markets if it's passed without significant changes."
He said if the budget was cleared the market was likely trade between 3,600-3,900 from its current 3,300-3,600 range.
Foreign investors were disturbed by the political developments but will not dump shares, analysts said.
"I don't see a major sell-off," said Bharat Iyer, market strategist at UBS Securities, the investment arm of Union Bank of Switzerland.
He said foreign investors put money into Indian stocks because of the long-term growth story and were unlikely to get out due to short-term political instability.
But fresh purchases would slow until the picture became clearer or till valuations became more attractive, analysts said. -- Bombay Newsroom, (91) 22 265 9000
